tone_statements.citation: Pacquement, Jean. 2018. The Nyo language spoken at Kut Kho Kan village (Loeng Nok Tha district, Yasothon province): A Language Documentation Research at Roi Et Rajabhat University. Sikkha Journal of Education (สิกขา วารสารศึกษาศาสตร์, Vongchavalitkul University) 5(2): 73-84.
tone_statements.quote: A more precise tone inventory will distinguish four or five tones in the smooth syllables and three tones in the checked syllables. The smooth syllables have a mid falling, then low rising tone (214) in the A1, A2, A3 cells, a low rising, then mid falling tone (231) in the A4 cell, a low rising, then mid level tone (233) in the B1, B2, B3 cells, and the C1 cell, and low rising tones in the B4 cell, and in the C2, C3, C4 cells (respectively a 25 tone, and a 15 tone). As for the checked syllables, they have a low rising, then mid level tone (233) in the DL1, DL2, DL3 cells, a low rising tone (13) in the DL4 cell, and the DS1, DS2, DS3 cells, and a low level tone (11) in the DS4 cell.

tone_statements.n_tones: 4-5 smooth-syllable tones + 3 checked-syllable tones (Kut Kho Kan)

tone_statements.quote: As far as tonal system is concerned, that of the "Phutai" is distinct from those of the "Lao" and the "Nyo". The "Phutai" systems found in this study still maintain the distinctive characteristics of the typical Phutai tonal system. The "Lao" systems all vary from the typical Lao tonal system while all except one of the Nyo systems also vary from the typical Nyo tonal system.

tone_statements.quote: “phonetically speaking, the Nyo tones in the twenty-six tambons are so distinctively different from each other that they produce twenty-six accents, These accents can be divided into three major dialects based on tonal systes, namely four-tone, five-tone, and sixetone systems. In addition, they can be divided into seven- sub-groups based on tone splits.

sources.note: First-hand F0-based Gedney tone-box analysis of Nyo speakers of Kut Kho Kan: 4-5 tones on smooth syllables (214 in A123, 231 in A4, 233 in B123+C1, rising 25 in B4, 15 in C234) and 3 on checked syllables (233 DL123, 13 DL4+DS123, 11 DS4); split B123-4, coalescence C1=DL123 and quasi-coalescence B4≈C234≈DL4; same split/merger pattern as Nyo of Sakon Nakhon but different tone shapes; reviews Koowatthanasiri 1981, Akharawatthanakun 2002, Pinkanok 2002, Chamberlain 1975/1984 on Nyo tones; a Dong Yen (Mukdahan) Nyo speaker shows real coalescence B4=C234=DL4.

sources.note: Auditory + instrumental comparison of tonal systems and tone phonetics in 3 Nyo, 3 Lao and 3 Phu Thai villages (150-item list from two analogous tone sets, 10 tokens x 15 words); establishes a 'typical Nyo tonal system' from earlier literature and finds all but one of the Nyo village systems deviate from it toward Lao, while some Lao systems have shifted toward Nyo; Phu Thai keeps its distinct system; many tones phonetically similar across the three groups.
